stem: Victoria is a 3-year-old girl with a history of two ICU admissions for asthma exacerbations. She is currently taking fluticasone (Flixotide) 500 micrograms three times daily. What comment would you make about the dose-response curve for inhaled corticosteroids (ICS)?

options.text: The dose response curve for inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) is relatively flat, such that little benefit is seen with doses above 500 µg fluticasone daily
The dose response curve for ICS is relatively steep, such that there is continued benefit with doses limited only by side effects
The dose response curve for ICS is variable, such that there is no relationship between dose and symptoms
The dose response curve for ICS is irrelevant to clinical care
The dose response curve for ICS is irrelevant for patients admitted to the intensive care unit

explanation: Inhaled corticosteroids have a relatively flat dose-response curve at higher doses: most benefit is achieved at low to moderate doses, with diminishing additional benefit and increasing risk of adverse effects as the dose rises. This is why escalating to very high doses often provides little extra clinical gain.

citations.title: Practice Quiz: Asthma Management: Medications and Devices - Part B

rationale: Preserve the existing options and mark the statement describing the flat dose-response curve of ICS as correct.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. This reflects the flat high-dose ICS dose-response curve and diminishing returns above moderate doses.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect. ICS do not have a steep dose-response curve with unlimited benefit up to side effects.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect. There is a dose-response relationship, although it becomes flatter at higher doses.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect. The dose-response curve is clinically important when choosing and stepping up treatment.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect. Prior ICU admission does not make the pharmacologic dose-response curve irrelevant.
